Climate-related information
The future effects of climate change, and their impact on Kiwibank, are highly 
uncertain. As a result, the climate-related information in this report is also subject 
to limitations, judgements and uncertainties, including in relation to the methods, 
data, tools, models, standards and frameworks used to prepare this report. 
These limitations, judgements and uncertainties mean that some information in

In particular, due to limited data availability, some of the disclosures in this

assume the reliability of third-party data and methods of analysis. Specific 
information about methods and assumptions and data and estimation 
uncertainty underlying the disclosures in this climate statement is included  
in the Appendices on pages 36 – 49.

Rautaki

Kiwibank is the largest Aotearoa New Zealand-owned bank, with $40.7 billion in 
total assets.1 Kiwibank’s founding vision was for Aotearoa New Zealand to have 
a real, relevant and credible alternative to offshore-owned banks. That informs 
our work and is reflected in our Purpose of Kiwi making Kiwi better off.
Kiwibank’s parent, Kiwi Group Capital Limited, is 100% owned by the Crown.2  3  
We are also a Certified B Corporation.

Kiwibank’s business model
Kiwibank operates a nationwide retail and business bank for personal customers 
and businesses. Kiwibank’s core product offerings include transactional products 
and services, savings accounts, credit cards and a range of lending solutions 
including home loans, commercial loans, asset finance and trade finance.
Kiwibank provides access to banking through digital channels, supported by  
a nationwide branch network (including our Local for Kiwibank service agents) 
and Aotearoa New Zealand contact centre. Kiwibank also offers access to 
specialists via its branches, Business Hubs, a network of mobile mortgage 
specialists and third-party advisers.
Kiwibank’s Purpose and strategy4
Our Purpose is Kiwi making Kiwi better off.
We have three focus areas for Purpose delivery:
Making tamariki (children) better off
Making Kiwi better off
Making Aotearoa New Zealand better off.
Our strategy is to continue to grow market share in retail and business banking 
as a purpose-led, challenger bank. Being the bank that more Kiwi and Kiwi 
businesses prefer to use for their banking, home lending and business needs 
(being Customers’ 1st Choice) is how we can have more impact to make Kiwi 
better off.
To be Customers’ 1st Choice, we are focused on the following:
Easy: Our customers can easily and quickly get things done
Accessible: Our customers can reach us when and how they need us
Expert: Our customers trust our expertise
Care: Our customers feel understood and cared for.

Transition plan aspects of our strategy
In our 2024 Climate Statement, we said we would disclose details in this 2025 
Climate Statement of our plan for mitigating and adapting to the effects of 
climate change, and transitioning to a low-carbon, climate-resilient economy 
(our Transition Plan). 
Since then, the Financial Markets Authority – Te Mana Tātai Hokohoko (FMA) 
has issued clarificatory guidance about the requirement in FY25 for climate 
reporting entities to disclose the transition plan aspects of their strategy.  
It specifies that “The Climate Standards do not mandate that [climate reporting 
entities] must have a transition plan, or set out any specific approach or process 
for transition planning...” 6 
We decided during FY25 to delay publication of a first, consolidated Transition 
Plan, to allow us more time to develop it. This means we have not yet fully 
developed our Transition Plan. Specifically:
We have not yet reassessed our strategic choices against the material 
climate risks and opportunities we identified in FY25. 
We have not yet formally linked our internal capital deployment  
and funding decision-making processes to the transition plan aspects 
of our strategy. 
These are elements of the fuller Transition Plan we are currently progressing. 
Because we are still developing Kiwibank’s first Transition Plan, we have not  
yet identified the extent to which any changes to our business model and 
strategy may be required. 
We have, however, started to position Kiwibank for its transition to a low-
emissions future by implementing climate-related targets, products, and risk 
controls. The most material of these are described below. 
We have had a Responsible Business Policy (RBP) in place since FY21. 
We updated our RBP and strengthened supporting processes and 
controls during FY25. Our RBP sets out how we will work with businesses 
that carry environmental, social and governance (ESG) risks.  
It specifically helps us manage transition risk in our lending decisions.  
It also applies more broadly to our suppliers and other financial 
institutions that we trade with (Treasury counterparties). Additionally:
–   Our RBP identifies Excluded and Sensitive sectors. We may work with 
businesses in Sensitive sectors if they are working to mitigate their 
ESG risk. 
–   RBP assessments of businesses in Sensitive sectors are integrated into 
our credit decision-making process. 
More information on our RBP, including detail about sectors identified 
as Excluded or Sensitive, is presented in Table 8 on page 24. 
We have offered sustainable finance products since FY23. Sustainable 
finance is one of our most material climate-related opportunities. 
More information on Kiwibank’s sustainable finance opportunity and 
activity is on page 31. In FY25 we progressed the development of our 
Sustainable Finance Framework, which is designed to strengthen 
our processes for determining which lending transactions qualify as 
sustainable finance.
We have been measuring and working to reduce some of our 
operational emissions since FY18. We have had reduction targets in 
place for the operational emissions we measure since FY21. (Refer 
to pages 28 – 29 for more about these targets and our performance 
against them.) These targets do not apply to our financed emissions. 
Our FY21 operational emissions reduction targets ended on 30 June 
2025. We have set new operational emissions reduction targets to 
2030. Refer to page 30 for more details. These reduction targets are 
integrated into Kiwibank’s strategic delivery plan, as business-level  
Key Performance Indicators (KPIs). 
We made progress in developing the transition plan aspects of our strategy  
in FY25. Specifically, we:
Established a Climate and ESG Advisory team to drive development 
and delivery of our first Transition Plan
Developed a workplan for Transition Plan delivery 
Evolved the measurement of our financed emissions to better 
understand where we could focus our efforts to support customers  
to reduce their emissions 
Undertook new climate scenario analysis to mature our understanding 
of Kiwibank’s climate risks and opportunities. These scenarios 
incorporated custom economic modelling and included more 
challenging climate conditions than envisaged by our FY24 scenarios. 
Refer to pages 13 – 16 for more information.

Methods, assumptions and limitations: identification 
of Kiwibank’s climate risks and opportunities over 
the short, medium and long term
Our FY25 identification and assessment of climate risks and opportunities were 
primarily informed by the outputs of our scenario analysis. Details of our scenario 
analysis process are on pages 13 – 16.
Our risk and opportunity identification is subject to uncertainty about how 
climate change will unfold, and the global and domestic transition pathways 
that may influence the nature and magnitude of future climate-related events.
Tables 3 and 4 on pages 10 – 12 (overleaf) present Kiwibank’s key climate risks 
and opportunities, including the time horizons over which we estimate they may 
arise. These tables also set out the categories of impact and financial impact 
we anticipate should these risks or opportunities materialise. We have not 
quantified financial impacts in FY25, relying on Adoption Provision 2.
Our short-term climate horizon aligns with our short- and medium-term  
strategic and capital deployment planning time horizons. Our medium-term 
climate horizon reflects the typical maximum term of our home loans. This year, 
we extended our long-term climate horizon by 21 years, to 2100, for deeper 
future insight.
Both our medium- and long-term climate horizons exceed our typical strategic 
and capital deployment planning time horizons. We consider that integration 
of a longer-term view of climate risks and opportunities can inform our shorter-
range strategic choices and capital deployment.
We have not reassessed Kiwibank’s strategic choices between now and 2033 
(being the end of Kiwibank’s strategic and capital planning time horizons) 
against the material climate risks and opportunities we identified this year.
Risks and opportunities as inputs to Kiwibank’s 
capital deployment and funding decision-making 
processes
We conducted our FY25 identification of climate risks and opportunities 
independently of our internal capital deployment and funding  
decision-making processes. 
We did not integrate climate risks and opportunities into our capital  
deployment processes in FY25. 
We integrated climate risks into our funding decision-making processes through 
our RBP. The RBP informs our decisions about which customers we will lend to 
in sectors that carry ESG risks. In combination with other policies, it specifically 
helps us manage transition-related credit risk in our lending.
We integrated climate opportunities into our funding decision-making  
processes by our continued provision of sustainable finance. See page 31  
for more information.

In FY25, we conducted a fresh assessment of Kiwibank’s material climate risks 
and opportunities across the short, medium and long term. We based this 
assessment on renewed climate scenario analysis and internal expertise.  
We identified a different set of climate risks and opportunities compared  
to the prior period.
Credit risk remains one of our most material financial climate risks, because our 
main business activity is lending to residential and business customers. Credit risk 
is the risk of customers or counterparties failing to meet their contractual 
payment obligations.
We have also identified the categories of impact we anticipate if our material 
climate risks or opportunities crystallise. We have not yet quantified those 
impacts. We did not conduct geographic or sectoral analysis of our climate risks

As the world transitions to a low-carbon economy, Kiwibank will need to align with evolving expectations of

Negative perception could result from Kiwibank transitioning either:

We consider that the scenarios we used are relevant and appropriate  
to assessing the resilience of Kiwibank’s business model and strategy to  
climate risks and opportunities because:
We designed them for Kiwibank’s unique context and lending  
portfolio composition. This meant focusing on factors impacting  
home and business lending customers and their assets in the  
Aotearoa New Zealand market.
They are based on generally accepted scenario archetypes (see  
Table 5 on page 15). We have not modified these archetypes, but we 
have drawn specific elements from them to ensure we have relevant 
information for Aotearoa New Zealand’s context and our driving forces.
The three scenarios (“Orderly”, “Too Little, Too Late” and “Hothouse 
World”) create a range of possible climate futures, with different levels 
of physical risk and transition risk present in each. For example, the 
“Hothouse World” scenario represents a very stressful physical impact 
scenario for Aotearoa New Zealand and Kiwibank, including tipping 
points such as a collapsing AMOC9 and melting Greenland ice shelf.  
The “Orderly” scenario introduces a high degree of short-term 
transition risk and lower physical risk. “Too Little, Too Late” features 
both high physical risk and high transition risk.
We designed our scenarios to consider the whole of our operations. The endpoint 
for each scenario is the year 2100.
We used New Zealand Banking Association – Te Rangapū Pēke (NZBA) banking-
sector scenarios to inform our decisions on driving forces, critical uncertainties, 
time horizons, shared socio-economic pathways (SSP) and the general trajectory 
of our three distinct scenarios. The focus on institutional and agricultural lending 
in the NZBA scenarios is not relevant to Kiwibank. Our entity-level scenarios 
allowed for a more nuanced view of impacts to home and business lending 
under a higher degree of climate stress.
In relation to the governance process used to oversee and manage the scenario 
analysis process, scenario narratives were approved by our Executive Risk 
Committee and noted by our Board-level Audit and Review Committee. Material 
climate risks and opportunities were noted by our Executive Risk Committee, and 
Board-level Audit and Risk Committee. 
Kiwibank uses climate scenario analysis to identify and assess climate risks and 
opportunities and their anticipated impacts. 
Climate scenarios are plausible, challenging descriptions of how the future may 
unfold. Climate scenario analysis systematically explores the potential impacts 
that the range of futures described in these scenarios could have on Kiwibank’s 
business model and strategy.
We built and analysed new scenarios in FY25. This was a stand-alone process 
and not integrated with our strategy processes. We engaged an external 
consultant (Deloitte) to help with scenario development and analysis, including 
providing data and modelling, facilitating scenario workshops and contributing 
to scenario narrative writing. We currently intend to refresh our scenarios at least 
every three years. No other external partners or stakeholders were involved.

Risk Management

Kiwibank has an integrated risk culture where responsibility for managing risk is 
embedded at every level of the bank. Each one of our kaimahi is responsible for 
identifying and controlling risks in their own area of work. We support them with 
training, as well as systems and procedures for monitoring and reporting actual 
or perceived risk issues.
Our risk management framework and risk domains
In FY25, we updated our Enterprise Risk Management Framework (ERMF), which 
guides our approach to identifying, assessing and managing Kiwibank’s risks. 
(See Fig. 7 (right).) This framework is underpinned by the Three Lines of Defence 
model, which clearly delineates responsibilities for risk ownership, oversight,  
and independent assurance. A fuller description of our ERMF components and 
Three Lines of Defence model can be found in our Disclosure Statement.21
We manage our risks by categorisation across eight Material Risks.22 Across 
these Material Risk categories, we categorise risks into 23 Risk Domains, and 
these include ESG and Climate Change from FY25. 
Our ERMF categorises climate change principally as a Strategic Risk. However, 
we also recognise that it is cross-cutting in nature, and inherent within all our 
other Material Risk categories. See Table 3 on pages 10 – 11 for detail about how 
we have identified climate risk across our Material Risks. 
Integrating climate risk into our risk management framework
We progressed integration of climate risk into our risk management framework 
by distinguishing ESG and Climate Change as a distinct Strategic Risk domain 
from FY25. This should support ready identification and assessment of climate 
risks within our overall risk view.
Prioritisation of climate risks relative to other types of risks
We did not formally prioritise individual climate risks relative to other enterprise 
risk types in FY25.

We have set new FY30 Operational Emissions Targets (FY30 OETs) to manage 
Kiwibank’s operational emissions from FY26. We intend to restate our base year

against our FY30 OETs in FY26. Our FY30 OETs do not include interim targets.

of our performance against them in this report. Refer to pages 28 – 29 (previous) 
for a description of our performance against our FY25 OERT.
We developed our FY30 OETs using guidance from the SBTi (noting that they 
have not been verified or approved by SBTi). Our adherence to SBTi guidance 
supports our view that these targets contribute to limiting global warming to 1.5°C 
(for Scope 1 and 2) and well below 2.0°C (for Scope 3). SBTi guidance informed our 
calculations to determine emissions pathways that would align with 1.5°C and well 
below 2.0°C, if achieved. Our FY30 OETs do not rely on offsets to be achieved.
Our carbon neutral ambition
In addition to our FY25 OERT, we set an ambition in FY22 to be a carbon-neutral 
business by FY25. Carbon neutrality means achieving a balance between the 
carbon we emit and the carbon we indirectly remove from the atmosphere by 
way of offsetting. It remains our ambition to achieve carbon neutrality. However, 
we decided not to purchase offsets to achieve this in FY25. This is because we did 
not identify purchase options in FY25 that align with our offsetting investment 
principles. We want to ensure our offsetting investment:
	▪
Remains in Aotearoa New Zealand, meaning our investment should be 
in a domestic project or projects only
	▪
Creates or supports new or additional carbon removals rather than 
financing a project that has already occurred.
We currently intend to reinvestigate our offsetting investment options from FY26.
Our partnership with Air New Zealand
Air travel emissions are a significant contributor to domestic and global 
emissions, and are one of Kiwibank’s most material Scope 3 emissions sources 
(excluding financed emissions). We anticipate that reducing our air travel 
emissions will remain a particular challenge as we grow our team and our 
business over the coming years.
We have entered into a partnership with Air New Zealand from August 2025 
to support its efforts to transition 10% of its aviation fuel supply to sustainable 
aviation fuel (SAF) by 2030. Kiwibank does not make any offsetting claim in FY25 
in relation to this investment.
SAF releases the same amount of carbon as regular aviation fuel when burnt 
in an aircraft engine. However, it has significantly lower lifecycle emissions 
because it is made from materials other than fossil fuels such as used cooking oil, 
household waste or forestry waste.31 Significant investment is needed to support 
the expansion of SAF production globally and domestically, and our current 
partnership with Air New Zealand is intended to support its efforts in this regard.

Detailed scenario narrative summaries, by time horizon
The detailed summary narratives below demonstrate how each scenario evolves over our three time horizons. These summaries are more detailed than those provided in Table 6 on page 16. The full narratives used in our scenario analysis process are 
significantly longer and more detailed, and are not reproduced in this report.
Orderly
2025 – 2030
A brief period of global inaction triggers social backlash as losses mount from 
more frequent and severe weather events. Governments around the world 
respond by enacting a combination of domestic fiscal policies, green economy 
stimulus packages and carbon pricing mechanisms, alongside international 
carbon border taxes. Aotearoa New Zealand prices carbon and other 
environmental externalities into the costs of production to avoid being left 
behind. This causes a temporary economic contraction.
A high and rapidly rising carbon price motivates households and businesses to 
transition. Demand increases for assets that reduce household emissions and 
improve resilience. Such assets include EVs, electric bikes, energy efficiency 
retrofits, and resilience projects. Businesses seek to transition quickly as export 
markets demand low-carbon products. Inflation is triggered as unprecedented 
demand for transition-related products and services increases costs. The high 
carbon price and swift transition produce winners and losers across the economy. 
NZ GDP falls in the short term. 
Aotearoa New Zealand sees very marginal increases in rainy days, rainfall 
intensity, drought risk and hot days. Scientists warn of rapidly approaching 
tipping points, and there is social backlash against inaction. The government 
provides climate hazard data for all. This enables the insurance industry to 
confidently and collectively move to risk-based pricing. Property prices decline 
in high-risk locations as a result. Some customers in risky locations struggle to 
afford adequate insurance cover, which sparks considerable public outrage 
and pressure on the government. In response, the Natural Hazards Commission 
coverage is expanded to maintain high insurance coverage rates.
 
2031 – 2050
Governments globally continue to implement strong and clear decarbonisation 
and resilience policies. GDP losses ease and Aotearoa New Zealand benefits 
from an increase in foreign direct investment. Household disposable income 
begins to improve. 
Early adopters are rewarded and laggards are punished as carbon prices soar 
to $774 per metric tonne. Industries and job markets shift in structure as a result. 
‘Just transition’ policies provide training and support to ensure the country is able 
to manage these shifts.
Severe weather events, floods and landslides occur with increasing intensity 
and frequency, causing people and communities to invest in adaptation and 
slowly retreat from risk-prone locations. This proactive action limits losses and 
damages.
Insurance prices escalate and coverage rates begin to decline in response to the 
rise in severe weather events. The government introduces regulation to prevent 
excessive price increases and policy cancellations. Insurers launch innovative 
products tailored to different risk profiles. 
Towards 2050, Aotearoa New Zealand declares the decarbonisation transition 
complete and the economy rebounds considerably.
 
2051 – 2100
The transition has fundamentally changed people’s relationship with 
consumption, resulting in less demand for manufactured goods. Kiwi move 
towards a shared economy via ‘libraries of things’. This causes many legacy 
manufacturing firms to be replaced with new ones focusing on core needs, 
services, recovery and resilience. 
Sea levels rise by 0.53 of a metre, drought conditions worsen, and severe weather 
events occur more frequently. However, global climate action halts temperature 
rise at 1.5°C and reverses it to 1.4°C. The worst-case scenario is avoided, and 
the physical impacts are manageable. Reinsurance remains stable as a result. 
Premiums mostly remain affordable and coverage rates are high, enabling 
timely recovery and rebuild efforts from severe weather events. However, house 
prices continue to decline over the period relative to baseline.
By 2100, Aotearoa New Zealand achieves a resilient and sustainable economy. 
Real household income is higher with lower unemployment and higher GDP, 
relative to all other scenarios.

Too Little, Too Late
2025 – 2030
The global average temperature rises 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels by 2030, 
yet international and domestic climate action regresses. Populist governments 
and major corporations weaken or abandon climate commitments, including 
emissions reduction targets and clean technology investments. Domestically, 
regulatory rollbacks undermine decarbonisation efforts across the private  
sector by reducing the number of climate-reporting entities. Banks and  
financial institutions withdraw from global climate alliances. Government 
climate plans remain unfunded and largely ignored. Agriculture remains  
exempt from emissions pricing. Local authorities lack the mandate to prevent 
risky developments, increasing the proportion of residents exposed to climate-
related hazards. 
A series of extreme weather events in Auckland, Wellington and Christchurch 
exposes the fragility of domestic infrastructure and financial systems. Insurers, 
overwhelmed by claims, raise premiums and withdraw coverage in high-risk 
areas. Banks face mounting losses from stranded assets. Insurance sector price 
increases drive declining coverage, both in terms of number of households 
insured and amount insured.
Economic instability follows. Weak climate policies and rising uncertainty cause 
GDP to fall and investment to slow. Productivity declines. Consumer demand  
for climate-resilient technologies remains low and industry lobbying further 
delays progress. 
Severe floods, landslides and droughts become more frequent and sea levels 
continue to rise. This highlights an urgent need for coordinated, long-term 
climate action.
 
2031 – 2050
Aotearoa New Zealand and several major economies have failed to meet  
their 2030 carbon targets. International widespread adoption of carbon border 
adjustment mechanisms increases Aotearoa New Zealand’s cost of capital and 
locks the country out of key export markets. In response, the country strengthens 
its climate action to regain market access. Initiatives include high emissions 
pricing (including for agriculture, aviation and shipping) and grant funding  
for business transitions. This sees a delayed but rapid transition, marked by  
high unemployment, declining disposable income, and increasing inflation. 
However, successful renegotiation of trade agreements eventually boosts 
exports and foreign capital inflows, helping to stabilise the economy and  
reduce unemployment.
The increasing frequency of climate-related disasters drives up infrastructure 
repair costs, leading to higher local taxes and inflation, which further reduce 
household disposable income. The government expands the national insurance 
scheme to cover flood risk and begins to provide high-quality climate risk data 
to support more accurate, risk-based insurance pricing. The increase in risk-
based pricing drives central and local governments to take adaptation action. 
However, this leads to affordability issues and a rise in negative equity and 
mortgage defaults, especially in high-risk areas. Insurers begin withdrawing 
from these areas and class actions are mounted against banks for knowingly 
lending in risky locations. 
Meanwhile, global decarbonisation efforts remain fragmented. Major emitters 
exit the Paris Agreement, leading to a projected overshoot of Net Zero  
targets. Supply chain disruptions, rising costs, and climate litigation further  
strain economies. Despite these challenges, Aotearoa New Zealand’s low-
carbon economy begins to show signs of recovery by the late 2040s, with 
improved household incomes, declining unemployment rates and increasing 
economic resilience.
 
2051 – 2100
The country experiences increasingly severe and frequent weather events 
by 2050. The global failure to limit warming to 1.5°C leads to escalating 
climate-related damages that far exceed government recovery capabilities. 
International trade collapses due to widespread civil unrest, resource shortages, 
and infrastructure failures. Aotearoa New Zealand is economically isolated. 
Infrastructure deteriorates under climate stress, contributing to falling property 
values. The domestic economy suffers as global economies fragment and 
foreign investment dries up. Rising interest rates give way to long-term economic 
decline. By 2100, productivity has decreased significantly, unemployment has 
soared, and household incomes have fallen. Carbon markets have stalled, and 
inequality has surged. The wealthy adapt and self-insure, while others face 
devastating losses from climate-related events.
Reinsurers pull out of the Aotearoa New Zealand market between 2050 and 
2060. As a result, insurance becomes increasingly unaffordable and is entirely 
unavailable by 2100. Property prices in high-risk locations consequently fall  
as a result. Homeowners demand accountability from the government. 
Soaring inflation limits access to resilient building materials, which deepens 
social inequality. Climate migration and managed retreat reshape population 
demographics and concentrate people in a few climate-resilient zones.  
Sea level rise renders many coastal areas uninhabitable, while slips and  
floods isolate remote communities. Sea levels have risen by 1.2 metres,  
droughts have intensified, and water prices have surged by 2100. The physical 
and economic toll of climate change continues to mount. There are widespread 
impacts on housing, employment, and national GDP. Social conflict grows as 
inequality soars.

Hothouse World
2025 – 2030
Global climate action has regressed significantly by 2030. This is driven by 
far-right political movements and corporate backtracking on environmental 
commitments. Aotearoa New Zealand prioritises economic growth over 
emissions reductions and adaptation. The Emissions Trading Scheme is left  
weak and ineffective. 
The government fails to implement a national adaptation strategy, leaving  
local councils without the tools to prevent development in risky locations, or to 
retreat from high-risk areas. Public awareness of climate risks remains low due  
to limited access to climate hazard data. Demand for sustainable finance 
products is minimal. Climate risk is poorly managed as a result. Financial 
institutions continue to fund vulnerable assets. 
Aotearoa New Zealand benefits from its relatively temperate climate and 
increased demand for exports as other countries suffer more immediate climate 
impacts. Its economy appears stable. However, severe weather events begin 
to hit major centres and expose the country’s lack of resilience. Insurance 
markets become strained. Premiums rise and coverage reduces in high-
risk areas. This leads to climate-related gentrification, as wealthier people 
relocate to safer zones. Social inequality deepens as low-income communities 
are left in vulnerable areas without adequate protection or recovery support. 
Consumer scepticism towards climate science limits investment in resilience. 
Rising sea levels, droughts and heatwaves begin to affect agriculture and water 
availability. An absence of strong leadership and coordinated policy responses 
leave the nation increasingly exposed to escalating climate and economic risks.
 
2031 – 2050
Aotearoa New Zealand spends little to nothing on proactive mitigation or 
adaptation. Governments are forced into reactive recovery and infrastructure 
repair spending as climate impacts occur. Taxes rise, economic growth slows, 
and unemployment increases as a result. Sea level rise, severe weather events, 
coastal erosion and rainfall increases begin to take their toll. Some roads are 
eventually destroyed and councils cannot afford to repair them. This results in 
major disruptions to the flow of goods and services across the country.
Physical impacts intensify. Coastal erosion, sea level rise, and extreme rainfall 
events damage homes and infrastructure, leaving many unable to be repaired 
or relocated. The compounding effects of inadequate planning, poor risk 
pricing, and worsening climate conditions push Aotearoa New Zealand into a 
prolonged period of economic decline and social instability. Climate migration 
strains already fragile infrastructure, leading to higher rates of homelessness 
and crime, and social unrest. Exploitation of climate migrants in low-wage,  
high-risk jobs becomes widespread. Consumer behaviour shifts toward 
immediate survival needs, with sustainable investments deprioritised. 
Reinsurance is withdrawn and general insurers progressively fold under  
the weight of high pay-outs and infrequent reprieves. The insurance sector 
collapses. This triggers housing market polarisation. Prices soar in low-risk  
areas and collapse in high-risk zones. Wealthier individuals invest in adaptation, 
while vulnerable communities are left exposed. This deepens social inequity. 
Mortgage defaults rise, banks incur losses, and public trust in financial 
institutions and government erodes.
 
2051 – 2100
Beginning in the 2050s, a series of climate tipping points are triggered that 
accelerate climate impacts. The AMOC collapses in 2057, leading to food 
shortages across Europe. Marine ecosystems and fisheries collapse. Aotearoa 
New Zealand is relatively shielded from ex-tropical cyclone impacts due to a 
poleward shift. However, it faces immense pressure from climate migration, 
strained infrastructure, and surging demand for agricultural exports.
The AMOC collapse also accelerates atmospheric CO2 build-up, intensifying 
cryosphere melt and sea level rise. By 2064, further tipping points, being  
Amazon dieback and permafrost thaw, cause a spike in global temperatures.  
A catastrophic 2 metres of sea level rise by 2100 submerges the nation’s ports, 
airports and much of its roading network. Aotearoa New Zealand is effectively 
cut off from the rest of the world. 
By 2100, the domestic economy suffers a $556 billion GDP loss (at net present 
value), with annual GDP shrinking by 27% compared with today. People are 
unable to repair and rebuild assets as climate damage increases and insurance 
becomes non-existent. Civil society fragments under the weight of economic 
hardship, corruption, and government failure. Climate ghettos emerge, 
disease spreads and infrastructure collapses. Eventually, civil disobedience, 
black markets and looting begin. People focus on survival. Household income 
plummets, supply chains are broken, and black markets dominate the economy. 
Inflation becomes rampant. People struggle to survive.
Physical impacts intensify, with sea level rise, extreme heat, and drought far 
exceeding earlier projections. Entire communities are cut off. Lives are lost when 
heat and humidity surpass survivability thresholds. The compounding effects of 
delayed action, failed governance, and underestimated risks leave Aotearoa 
New Zealand and the world grappling with a future defined by irreversible 
climate collapse.

has been a material change during the reporting year to the measurement or 
calculation of emissions. This may include material changes in emission factors 
(including updates). Any structural change to the Kiwibank Group (including 
acquisitions and divestments) will trigger a base year review.
Base year recalculation and restatement may be necessary following a 
methodological change, including addition of new sources to the inventory that 
are part of the set target. Whether recalculation and restatement are necessary 
and possible will depend on an assessment of:
The nature of the methodological improvement 
Data availability and quality.
Operational control 
We take an operational control approach to measuring Kiwibank’s emissions. 
We reviewed our operational boundary in FY25 by mapping the entities  
and business activities over which Kiwibank has operational control.  
We define operational control as Kiwibank having full authority to introduce  
and implement its operating policies over an activity.
We also include in our inventory selected indirect Scope 3 emissions over which 
Kiwibank does not have operational control, but which are generated as a  
result of Kiwibank’s business activities. An example is emissions created by  
our air travel. 
We have excluded some sources of emissions that are within our operational 
control. A list of excluded FY25 emissions sources is set out in Table 23 on pages 
45 – 46.
Intensity metric calculation method
We have applied an intensity metric, being Kiwibank’s emissions per dollar  
of operating revenue. This measurement is set out in Table 9 on page 27.
The calculation is total emissions divided by dollars of operating revenue  
for the year ended 30 June in the relevant financial year.
Other than the base year measurement, the intensity metric calculation method, 
or where otherwise described, the information in this Appendix Operational

Measurement standards applied
We have measured and prepared our operational emissions in accordance with 
The Greenhouse Gas Protocol: A Corporate Accounting and Reporting Standard, 
Revised Edition and the Greenhouse Gas Protocol: Corporate Value Chain (Scope 
3) Accounting and Reporting Standard (GHG Protocol). We have disclosed our 
operational emissions in compliance with the Aotearoa New Zealand Climate 
Standards (NZ CS).42
Emission factors
We primarily use Ministry for the Environment – Manatū Mō Te Taiao  
(Ministry for the Environment) 2025 emission factors. These are based on the 
100-year Global Warming Potential (GWP) values (GWP100) for the IPCC’s Fifth 
Assessment Report (AR5). 
For a small number of emission sources, there are no applicable Ministry for the 
Environment factors. For those, we have used 2025 UK Government Greenhouse 
Gas Conversion factors for Company Reporting (2025 UK GHG Conversion factors). 
These are based on GWP100 for AR5. 
Emission factors used for each source are set out in Table 22 on pages 42 – 44.
Emissions quantification is inherently uncertain because the scientific knowledge 
used to determine emission factors and the values needed to combine emissions 
of different gases is incomplete.
Base year measurement
Our base year measurement period, for emissions reduction targets set to  
FY25 and new targets set to FY30, is from 1 July 2020 to 30 June 2021 (FY21).
We selected FY21 as our base year because:
It is the earliest relevant point in time for which Kiwibank has  
reliable data
It covers 12 consecutive months
It is an accurate representation of Kiwibank’s typical emissions profile.

Inland flood risk for home lending: methods, 
assumptions and uncertainties
We used Moody’s RMS™ probabilistic inland flood models, in combination with 
Valocity™ property data, to allocate Flood Risk Scores for our Home Lending 
Securities and Home Lending Exposure. These scores reflect potential property 
damage from inland flood events in Aotearoa New Zealand.
Our assessment of inland flood risk to our Home Lending Securities and  
Home Lending Exposure is subject to the following limitations and uncertainties:
Reliance on third-party data: We have used data and modelling 
approaches we consider credible. However, actual exposure of our 
Home Lending Securities and Home Lending Exposure to inland flood 
risk is higher or lower than indicated.
Modelling assumptions and data availability: Moody’s RMS™ models 
incorporate flood defence and mitigation measures only where 
publicly-available data exists. Building specifications are considered 
where reasonably available. 
Incomplete data coverage: Due to data quality limitations, we were 
unable to match all Home Lending Securities and Home Lending 
Exposure to inland flood risk data. The analysis covers 92.3% of Home 
Lending Securities (FY24: 91.0%) and 92.2% of Home Lending Exposure  
(FY24: 91.2%).
Property use and occupancy: All properties are treated equally 
regardless of use (for example, owner-occupied or rental properties). 
Different occupancy types may have varying levels of resilience or 
access to insurance and adaptation resources.
Insurance coverage: Properties at risk are assumed to have adequate 
insurance coverage. Actual insurance uptake, coverage limits, and 
exclusions are not factored into the exposure analysis.
Due to data limitations, we have not considered:
Other location-specific elements that may impact inland flood severity, 
such as flood depth or water velocity
The interaction of inland flood risk with coastal flood risk. 
Coastal flood risk for home lending: methods, 
assumptions and uncertainties
We used coastal flooding data from NIWA™ and property location data  
from Valocity™ to assess the exposure of our home lending portfolio to  
coastal flood risk.
Our assessment of the coastal flood risk exposure is subject to the following 
limitations and uncertainties:
Reliance on third-party data: We have relied on third-party data that 
we consider credible. However, projections of future climate change 
impacts are inherently uncertain. As a result, the actual exposure of 
our Home Lending Securities and Home Lending Exposure to coastal 
flooding may be higher or lower than indicated.
Incomplete data coverage: Due to data quality limitations, we were 
unable to match all Home Lending Securities and Home Lending 
Exposure to coastal flood risk data. The analysis covers 92.6% of Home 
Lending Securities (FY24: 91.5%) and 92.6% of Home Lending Exposure 
(FY24: 91.9%).
Lack of property-specific risk modifiers: Our analysis does not account 
for building characteristics that may influence flood risk, such as 
elevation, foundation height, or construction materials. This may result 
in over- or underestimation of actual property-level risk. Different 
occupancy types may have varying levels of resilience or access to 
insurance and adaptation resources.
Insurance coverage: Properties at risk are assumed to have adequate 
insurance coverage. Actual insurance uptake, coverage limits, and 
exclusions are not factored into our exposure analysis.
Sea level rise data constraints: NIWA™’s sea level rise projections 
are provided in 10 cm increments. In FY25, we did not have access to 
projections beyond 1 metre. Accordingly, our analysis begins at  
20 cm in 2030 and extends to 2050.
Due to data limitations, we have not considered:
Other location-specific elements that may impact coastal flood 
severity, such as flood depth or wave velocity
The interaction of coastal flood risk with inland flood risk.

included enquiries, observation of processes performed, inspection of documents, 
analytical procedures, evaluating the appropriateness of quantification methods 
and reporting policies, and agreeing or reconciling with underlying record.  
Given the circumstances of the engagement, in performing the procedures listed 
above:

We evaluated the Group’s assessment of the Group’s organisational and 
operational boundaries; 
• 
We obtained, through enquiries, an understanding of the Group’s control 
environment, processes and information systems relevant to the preparation 
of the Scope 1, Scope 2 and selected Scope 3 disclosures. We did not evaluate 
the design of particular control activities or obtain evidence about their 
implementation; 
• 
We evaluated whether the Group’s methods for developing estimates are 
appropriate. Our procedures did not include testing the data on which the 
estimates are based or separately developing our own estimates against 
which to evaluate the Group’s estimates; 
• 
We performed analytical procedures on particular emission categories by 
scanning for anomalies or comparing the actual GHGs emitted on a monthly 
basis against a trend and made enquiries of management to obtain 
explanations for any significant differences identified; 
• 
We tested a limited number of items to, or from, supporting records, as 
appropriate;

We assessed the appropriateness of all in-scope emission factor sources and

• 
We inquired with management on the nature of the restatement to base year
